WASHINGTON (CNN) -- The government is warning that taking the psoriasis drug Raptiva could result in serious brain infection and even death. Raptiva may cause a serious brain infection called progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. The Food and Drug Administration cited three confirmed cases, and a possible fourth, of people diagnosed with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) after being treated with Raptiva. "Three of those patients have died," the FDA said in a public health advisory. "All four patients were treated with the drug for more than three years." None was receiving other treatments that suppress the immune system. Raptiva's product labeling was revised in October to highlight a boxed warning about the risks of life-threatening infections, including PML. "At that time, the FDA directed Genentech, the manufacturer, to develop a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS) to include a medication guide to educate patients about the drug's risks," the FDA's advisory says. In the advisory, issued Thursday, the FDA highlighted the confirmed cases and promised to "take appropriate steps" to ensure that Raptiva's risks do not outweigh its benefits. The FDA also said it will ensure that patients "are clearly informed of the signs and symptoms of PML" and that health care professionals "carefully monitor patients for the possible development of PML." Overseas, the European Medicines Agency has gone further, recommending that no new prescriptions for Raptiva be issued and that patients taking the drug talk to their doctors about an alternative. On Thursday it asked the European Commission to make that recommendation legally binding. The group's Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use determined "that the benefits of Raptiva no longer outweigh its risks, because of safety concerns, including the occurrence of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in patients taking the medicine." It said patients who have been treated with the drug should be "closely monitored for neurological symptoms and symptoms of infection." "Patients who are currently taking Raptiva should not stop treatment abruptly, but should make an appointment with their doctor to discuss the most appropriate replacement treatment," the agency said. Raptiva, a once-weekly injection for adults with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis, works by suppressing T-cells -- cells that help fight infection -- in the immune system. Those cells cause the skin inflammation associated with psoriasis. By suppressing T-cells, Raptiva "decreases the function of the immune system, which increases a patient's susceptibility to infections," the FDA said. The National Institutes of Health says the prognosis for PML "remains grim; the disease usually lasts for months and 80 percent die within the first six months, although spontaneous improvement has been reported. Those who survive PML can be left with severe neurological disabilities." Around 6 million to 7 million Americans have psoriasis, which is incurable, the NIH says.

**Title:** The Rise and Fall of Raptiva: How a Fatal Brain Infection Led to the Withdrawal of a Promising Psoriasis Drug

Raptiva (generic name *efalizumab*), a biologic medication once hailed as an innovative treatment for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, became the center of a major drug safety crisis after being linked to a rare and frequently fatal brain infection. Designed to suppress specific immune cells responsible for skin inflammation, the drug successfully alleviated symptoms for thousands of patients. However, this intentional suppression of the immune system carried a devastating, unintended consequence: it left long-term users vulnerable to opportunistic infections that the body could no longer fight off.

The primary threat associated with Raptiva was Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML), a destructive neurological condition caused by the reactivation of the John Cunningham (JC) virus. While the JC virus remains dormant and harmless in most healthy individuals, an immunocompromised system allows it to attack the brain's white matter, destroying the myelin sheath that protects nerve cells. PML leads to severe cognitive and physical impairment, often progressing rapidly to paralysis, dementia, and death.

As clinical reports began to link Raptiva to PML, health authorities on both sides of the Atlantic took aggressive action. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and European regulators issued urgent public health advisories to alert healthcare providers and patients of the emerging danger. In response, regulators ordered immediate revisions to product labeling, mandating the inclusion of a "Black Box Warning"—the FDA’s strongest safety alert—and requiring strict Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies (REMS) to ensure doctors weighed the drug's severe risks before prescribing it.

The crisis intensified when the FDA formally confirmed that three patients who had been taking Raptiva continuously for more than three years had died from PML. A fourth suspected case further heightened alarm. These deaths exposed a critical pattern: the risk of contracting PML appeared to rise significantly with prolonged, uninterrupted exposure to the drug. Because plaque psoriasis is a chronic, non-life-threatening skin condition, the discovery that long-term treatment could lead to a fatal brain disease fundamentally reshaped how regulators viewed the drug's safety profile.

This revelation proved to be the tipping point, particularly in Europe. Evaluating the accumulated safety data, the European Medicines Agency (EMA) concluded that the risk-benefit balance for Raptiva had collapsed. European officials declared that the drug’s modest clinical benefits no longer outweighed its life-threatening risks. Consequently, they recommended the immediate suspension of Raptiva’s marketing authorization across Europe, advising physicians to stop issuing new prescriptions and to safely transition existing patients to alternative therapies.

Shortly after the European recommendation and mounting pressure from the FDA, the drug's manufacturer, Genentech (a member of the Roche Group), announced a voluntary worldwide withdrawal of Raptiva from the market in April 2009. Patients were instructed not to stop taking the medication abruptly—due to the risk of severe psoriasis flare-ups—and were monitored closely by physicians for signs of neurological decline long after discontinuing the treatment.

The fall of Raptiva remains a landmark case in modern pharmacovigilance. It highlights the profound challenges of managing targeted biologic therapies and serves as a lasting reminder of the critical need for long-term safety monitoring when using immune-suppressing drugs to treat chronic, non-fatal illnesses.

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — Health authorities in the United States and Europe are issuing urgent warnings regarding the popular psoriasis drug Raptiva, citing evidence linking the medication to a rare, often fatal viral brain infection.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMEA) both released safety alerts highlighting the risk of Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy, or PML, in patients taking the drug. 

PML is a devastating neurological disease caused by a common virus that is typically kept in check by a healthy immune system. However, in patients whose immune systems are suppressed—such as those taking targeted biologic therapies like Raptiva—the virus can reactivate, destroying the protective coating around nerve cells in the brain. 

Symptoms of PML include confusion, loss of balance, difficulty speaking, vision loss, and weakness in the limbs. The disease usually leads to severe disability or death within months.

### Divergent regulatory actions

While both agencies agree on the severity of the threat, European regulators have taken a more aggressive stance. 

The EMEA’s Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use recommended suspending the marketing authorization for Raptiva across the European Union, concluding that the drug's benefits no longer outweigh its severe risks. 

"The safety profile of Raptiva shows a risk of serious infections, including fatal PML," the European agency said in a statement, noting that the modest benefits seen in psoriasis patients do not justify the risk of a fatal brain disease.

In the United States, the FDA is stopping short of an immediate ban, but is requiring manufacturer Genentech to highlight the risk with a "Black Box" warning—the agency’s strongest drug safety alert. The FDA is also requiring the company to implement a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) to ensure patients and healthcare providers are fully educated about the dangers.

At least three confirmed cases of PML in patients taking Raptiva have been reported, two of which were fatal, according to regulatory filings. All patients had been on the medication for more than three years.

### A delicate balancing act for patients

Raptiva, known generically as efalizumab, was approved in 2003 to treat moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, a chronic autoimmune skin condition that causes red, scaly patches. The drug works by blocking specific immune system cells (T-cells) that cause the skin inflammation typical of psoriasis. 

However, by suppressing those T-cells, the drug leaves the body vulnerable to opportunistic pathogens like the JC virus, which causes PML.

Medical experts are urging patients currently taking Raptiva not to panic, but to take immediate action. Crucially, doctors warn that patients should **not** stop taking the medication abruptly.

"Suddenly stopping Raptiva can lead to a severe, explosive rebound flare-up of psoriasis symptoms," warned CNN Chief Medical Correspondent Dr. Sanjay Gupta. "Patients need to contact their dermatologist immediately to discuss a safe transition strategy to an alternative therapy."

### The future of Raptiva

Genentech, a subsidiary of Roche, stated that it is working closely with global regulatory agencies to update safety information and evaluate the drug's future. 

"Patient safety is our top priority," Genentech said in a statement, noting that it has sent letters to healthcare professionals advising them of the updated safety protocols and risk factors.

With European regulators moving toward a full ban and American authorities tightening restrictions, industry analysts predict the future of Raptiva is severely compromised. The drug is part of a broader class of biologic treatments, though regulators emphasize that the current PML warnings apply specifically to Raptiva.

**HEALTH REPORT: Psoriasis Drug Raptiva Withdrawn Globally Over Fatal Brain Infection Risks**

**WASHINGTON** — Genentech’s prominent psoriasis medication, Raptiva, has been pulled from major global markets following a series of fatal brain infections, shedding light on the dangerous trade-offs of immune-suppressing biologic therapies and highlighting stark differences in how health regulators in the United States and Europe respond to drug safety crises.

At the center of the health risk is Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML), a rare, incurable, and usually fatal viral infection of the central nervous system. The outbreak of PML cases among Raptiva patients prompted emergency warnings, regulatory suspensions, and ultimately the voluntary withdrawal of the drug by its manufacturer.

---

### How Raptiva Works

Approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2003, Raptiva (generic name: *efalizumab*) was hailed as a targeted biologic therapy for adults suffering from moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. 

Psoriasis is a chronic autoimmune condition in which the body’s immune system mistakenly attacks healthy skin cells, causing rapid skin cell turnover that leads to painful, inflamed patches. 

Raptiva was designed to disrupt this process by acting as an immunosuppressant. The drug works by binding to a specific protein on the surface of T-cells—a type of white blood cell central to the body's immune response. By blocking these T-cells from interacting with endothelial cells and migrating into the skin, Raptiva successfully prevented the cascade of inflammation that causes psoriasis plaques.

However, the drug’s strength was also its fatal flaw. By broad-spectrum suppression of T-cell activity, Raptiva crippled a vital layer of the patient's immune defense, leaving the body incapable of fighting off opportunistic pathogens that healthy immune systems easily control.

---

### The Fatal PML Link and FDA Warnings

The crisis escalated when post-marketing surveillance revealed that long-term use of Raptiva created a window of vulnerability for the John Cunningham (JC) virus. 

The JC virus is a common pathogen present in a large portion of the general population, where it typically lies dormant and harmless in the kidneys or bone marrow. However, in patients whose immune systems are severely compromised by drugs like Raptiva, the virus can reactivate and travel to the brain. Once there, it attacks oligodendrocytes—the cells responsible for producing myelin, the protective sheath surrounding nerve fibers. The resulting disease, PML, leads to irreversible brain tissue damage, severe neurological disability, and death.

By late 2008 and early 2009, the FDA confirmed at least three fatal cases of PML in patients taking Raptiva, all of whom had been on the medication for more than three years. None of the patients had other underlying conditions that would explain such severe immune impairment. 

In February 2009, the FDA issued a public health advisory and mandated its strongest possible safety alert—a "Black Box Warning"—to be added to Raptiva’s packaging, warning physicians of the heightened risk of PML and other severe opportunistic infections.

---

### Transatlantic Divide: EMEA vs. FDA Responses

While both American and European officials recognized the danger, their regulatory strategies diverged significantly in speed and severity.

**The European Response:**
The European Medicines Agency (EMEA, now the EMA) adopted a swift, precautionary stance. In February 2009—the same month the FDA merely added a boxed warning—the EMEA’s Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) formally recommended the **immediate suspension** of Raptiva’s marketing authorization across the European Union. 

European regulators concluded that the risk-benefit balance for Raptiva was no longer positive. They reasoned that because plaque psoriasis is a non-fatal condition, exposing patients to a highly lethal brain infection like PML was medically unacceptable, especially when alternative treatments were available. 

**The U.S. Response:**
The FDA initially pursued a more conservative, phased approach. Rather than pulling the drug off the market immediately, the agency mandated a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) and updated safety labeling to inform doctors and patients of the risks. 

However, as public concern mounted and European markets shut down, Genentech (a member of the Roche Group) announced in April 2009 that it would voluntarily initiate a phased market withdrawal of Raptiva in the United States. The FDA approved the phased recall strategy to allow physicians time to transition patients to alternative therapies safely, as abruptly stopping Raptiva was known to cause severe, explosive rebounds of psoriasis symptoms.

---

### Aftermath and Legacy

The withdrawal of Raptiva stands as a cautionary milestone in the era of biological therapeutics. While targeted immunotherapies have revolutionized the treatment of autoimmune diseases, the Raptiva tragedy reinforced a critical lesson for pharmacology: suppressing the immune system to treat non-life-threatening chronic conditions carries profound risks that require vigilant, long-term monitoring.

Health authorities continue to advise any former Raptiva patients to monitor for potential neurological symptoms—such as confusion, dizziness, loss of balance, or difficulty speaking—and to consult their healthcare providers immediately if such symptoms arise.

**SPECIAL REPORT**

# From Promise to Peril: How Fatal Brain Infection Concerns Pulled Psoriasis Drug Raptiva Off the Market

**WASHINGTON** — In April 2009, biotech giant Genentech, in coordination with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), officially announced the voluntary phased withdrawal of the psoriasis drug Raptiva (efalizumab) from the U.S. market. The decision capped a dramatic fallout surrounding the once-promising biological therapy, following public health advisories that linked the medication to a rare, destruction-causing, and often fatal brain infection known as Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML).

The story of Raptiva serves as a landmark case study in drug safety, highlighting the delicate balance regulatory agencies must strike between managing chronic immune conditions and mitigating life-threatening side effects from biologic therapies.

---

### The Rise of Raptiva

Approved by the FDA in late 2003, Raptiva was heralded as a breakthrough for adults suffering from moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis—a painful autoimmune condition characterized by thick, red, scaly patches on the skin. 

Raptiva was designed as a humanized monoclonal antibody. It worked by suppressing the body’s immune response—specifically targeting and blocking T-cells, a type of white blood cell. By inhibiting T-cell activation and preventing them from migrating to the skin, Raptiva effectively halted the chronic inflammation that triggers psoriasis flare-ups. 

For thousands of patients, the weekly self-administered injection offered significant relief. However, the mechanism that made the drug effective—dampening the immune system—also opened the door to dangerous opportunistic infections.

---

### The Crisis Unfolds: The Link to PML

While clinical trials showed Raptiva was generally well-tolerated in the short term, concerns began to emerge after years of real-world, long-term use. 

The turning point occurred in late 2008 and early 2009, when the FDA received reports of patients on long-term Raptiva therapy developing Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML). PML is a devastating disease of the central nervous system that attacks the brain's white matter.

By February 2009, the FDA had confirmed three cases of PML in patients taking Raptiva, two of which had resulted in death. A fourth suspected case was under investigation. Crucially, all affected patients had been taking the drug continuously for more than three years.

In response, the FDA issued a stringent **Public Health Advisory** and mandated a prominent "Boxed Warning"—the agency’s strongest safety warning—highlighting the elevated risk of life-threatening infections, including PML. 

---

### Official FDA Response and Quotes

As the danger became clear, health authorities determined that the drug's risks far outweighed its benefits, given that psoriasis—while debilitating—is not a fatal disease.

In a public statement accompanying the February 2009 health advisory, **Dr. Janet Woodcock**, then-director of the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER), addressed the escalating safety concerns:

> *"The FDA is highlighting these risks to health care professionals and patients because PML is a serious, debilitating, and often fatal disease. Physicians should carefully evaluate the risk-benefit profile of Raptiva before prescribing it to patients."*

Two months later, as Genentech initiated the market withdrawal, the FDA issued a follow-up directive urging doctors not to start any new patients on Raptiva and to begin transitioning existing patients off the medication.

> *"The risks of serious, life-threatening infections associated with Raptiva outweigh the drug’s benefits for patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis,"* the FDA declared in its April 2009 withdrawal release, adding that patients abruptly stopping the medication should be monitored closely for severe rebound flare-ups of their psoriasis.

---

### Understanding PML: Pathophysiology and Prognosis

Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML) is a rare viral infection of the central nervous system caused by the **John Cunningham (JC) virus**. 

* **The Pathogen:** The JC virus is surprisingly common, present in an inactive, dormant state in an estimated 50% to 70% of the general adult population. In individuals with healthy immune systems, the virus is kept in check naturally and causes no symptoms or harm.
* **The Mechanism:** When a drug like Raptiva suppresses T-cell activity over an extended period, the immune system loses its ability to keep the JC virus latent. The virus reactivates, travels to the brain, and infects oligodendrocytes—the cells responsible for producing myelin, the protective fatty sheath around nerve fibers. 
* **Symptoms:** As myelin is destroyed, brain signals are disrupted. Patients experience rapidly progressing neurological symptoms, including severe memory loss, confusion, loss of coordination (ataxia), difficulty speaking, visual impairment, partial paralysis, and seizures.

#### Prognosis for PML
The prognosis for PML is notoriously grim:

1. **High Mortality Rate:** Historically, PML carries a mortality rate of **30% to 50%** within the first few months of diagnosis. 
2. **Lack of Targeted Antivirals:** There is no known direct antiviral cure or specific treatment for the JC virus. The primary medical intervention is to immediately cease the immunosuppressive medication (or restore immune function), allowing the body to fight off the virus.
3. **Permanent Neurological Damage:** Among those who survive PML, the majority are left with severe, irreversible neurological disabilities and permanent brain tissue loss. 

---

### The Aftermath and Legacy

Genentech’s decision to execute a phased withdrawal—concluding fully in June 2009—was designed to prevent a phenomenon known as "psoriasis rebound," where stopping the drug abruptly could cause an extreme, sometimes life-threatening surge in skin inflammation.

The downfall of Raptiva altered the landscape of biologic medicine. It served as a critical wake-up call for dermatologists, rheumatologists, and regulatory bodies regarding the cumulative risks of long-term immunosuppression. 

Today, while newer and safer biologic drugs (such as IL-17 and IL-23 inhibitors) have largely replaced earlier therapies, the memory of Raptiva's sudden exit remains a powerful reminder of how subtle disruptions to the human immune system can yield devastating consequences.

**FDA demands strict safety plan, warning guide for psoriasis drug Raptiva over fatal brain infection risk**

**WASHINGTON (CNN) --** The U.S. Food and Drug Administration is requiring a comprehensive safety plan and a detailed Medication Guide for patients taking the psoriasis drug Raptiva, citing an increased risk of life-threatening infections, including a rare and often fatal brain disease.

The FDA's mandate requires the drug's manufacturer, Genentech, to submit a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) to ensure that the benefits of the medication continue to outweigh its severe risks. 

At the center of the agency's heightened concern is Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML), a devastating neurological condition caused by the reactivation of a common, usually dormant virus in the body. PML attacks the central nervous system, destroying the protective myelin sheath that covers nerve cells in the brain. The disease leads to severe disability and is frequently fatal.

Symptoms of PML can mimic a stroke or multiple sclerosis and include progressive weakness on one side of the body, clumsiness, vision changes, confusion, and memory loss. 

Raptiva (efalizumab) was approved in 2003 to treat moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, a chronic autoimmune skin condition. The biologic medication works by suppressing specific T-cells in the immune system to halt the rapid overproduction of skin cells that causes painful, scaly patches. However, by dampening the body's immune defenses, Raptiva leaves patients uniquely vulnerable to opportunistic infections that a healthy immune system would normally fight off.

Under the new FDA requirements, a paper Medication Guide must be handed directly to patients every time a Raptiva prescription is filled or refilled. The guide outlines the warning signs of PML and other serious side effects in plain language, instructing patients to monitor their health closely and report any unusual symptoms to their doctors immediately. 

In addition to PML, the FDA noted that Raptiva has been linked to other severe adverse events, including high-grade bacterial infections, viral infections, tuberculosis, severe blood platelet shortages (thrombocytopenia), and hemolytic anemia.

Federal health officials emphasized that while the new safety measures are critical, patients currently taking Raptiva should not stop their medication abruptly. Suddenly discontinuing the drug can trigger a severe, widespread rebound flare-up of psoriasis that may require hospitalization.

"Patients taking Raptiva must be fully informed of these rare but severe risks so they and their doctors can make educated decisions about their treatment," the FDA stated, advising anyone taking the drug to consult their dermatologist or healthcare provider to evaluate whether they should remain on the therapy.
